highlights.quote: Aggression is a useful word only when it is made to carry less.
highlights.judgment: The book's controlling move stated with real economy; earns the definitional chapter that follows.

highlights.quote: The bones establish a violent meeting; they do not establish the institution that directed it.
highlights.judgment: Exemplary evidential discipline — and also the single sentence-shape the book reuses dozens of times.

highlights.quote: A ration is a small administrative decision. It says that a person belongs to a category, that food is held elsewhere, and that an official may release a measured amount according to a schedule.
highlights.judgment: Best kind of specificity: an institution explained through the paperwork that constitutes it.

highlights.quote: The first bones had come from the riverbank in 1997, when an amateur archaeologist named Detlef Jantzen found a human upper-arm bone
highlights.judgment: Internal contradiction — Jantzen is the state archaeologist in the 2009 scene two paragraphs earlier; a factual seam left unrepaired.

highlights.quote: By his own account, a man who crossed that passage would have seen the far bank only through reeds and spray.
highlights.judgment: "By his own account" attached to a hypothetical person: the dramatised openings occasionally borrow the authority of testimony they do not have.

highlights.quote: A wall required commands before it could protect. A ration required a clerk before it could feed. A boundary required a claimant before it could become a reason for war.
highlights.judgment: Powerful once, but this triadic anaphoric cadence closes at least eight chapters and becomes an audible tic.

highlights.quote: The same administrative form—a list, a permit, an allocation, an order—could sustain life in one setting and prepare destruction in another.
highlights.judgment: The comparative payoff the book is built for: British ration book against Ottoman deportation order, argued rather than asserted.

highlights.quote: The hand can be similar; the world directing it is not.
highlights.judgment: Aphoristic closer of a kind repeated at nearly every chapter end; the thesis gets restated more often than it gets advanced.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Every chapter opens with a cinematic reconstructed scene (named actor, weather, hands, small object) before any argument begins — an identical curtain-raiser across fifteen chapters.
instances: The trowel struck something that was not stone.
Oliver Cromwell was lifting his hat when the first royalist guns opened from the ridge above Naseby.

recurringPatterns.pattern: The negative-verdict antithesis: "X shows/establishes A; it does not show/establish B." Used to police evidence, but so uniform that the epistemic caution reads as a template rather than a judgment.
instances: The material record supports mass killing in a defended settlement; it does not supply a single motive.
The fire records an assault more firmly than it records its cause.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Chapters end with an anaphoric list of institutions substituted for people, then an aphoristic one-line moral.
instances: A person may strike in anger. A household may raid. A state may punish. An army may wage war. A regime may organise atrocity.
Human beings supplied anger, courage, grief, and fear. Cities, councils, temples, and imperial offices decided whether those forces became obligation, punishment, sacrifice, or peace.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Mid-chapter procedural enumerations — a numbered catalogue of signs or stages walked through one flat paragraph each — which stall the narrative and flatten the prose into a manual.
instances: A catalogue of archaeological signs begins with fortifications.
Selection came first. ... Then came concentration. ... At the destination, provincial officials distributed land, tools, seed, housing, or rations

recurringPatterns.pattern: The object-versus-office couplet, in which a material thing is granted force and then denied agency in the next clause.
instances: The weapon supplied force; an office selected its target.
The object supplied movement. An office supplied direction.

summary: This is a serious, intellectually disciplined comparative history whose thesis — that aggression is a family of acts whose scale and targets are made by offices, records and institutions rather than by an unchanging human nature — is stated early and genuinely tested across fifteen chapters from Tollense to Benghazi. Its strongest quality is evidential honesty: it repeatedly names what a mass grave, a stele, a ration tablet, a coroner's file or a parish register can and cannot support, and the closing chapter turns that scruple into an argument about the limits of comparison itself. Specificity is high and rarely decorative; the Wannsee, Barbados code, Tophane arsenal and Native Land Act sections are excellent. The costs are formal. Every chapter runs the same shape — dramatised opening scene, document, paired comparison, anaphoric institutional coda — and the sentence-level signature ("X establishes A; it does not establish B") recurs so often that caution starts to read as reflex rather than thought. Pacing suffers most in the enumerative middles, where catalogues of archaeological signs or deportation stages replace argument with inventory, and one small factual seam (Jantzen appearing as both the 2009 excavator and the 1997 amateur finder) survives into the opening pages. Light revision — thinning the closers, varying the chapter architecture, cutting perhaps a tenth of the restatement — would leave a genuinely accomplished book.
